content:
First principles feel slow, but JEE loves testing them. One clean rule beats memorising twenty derivatives. Master the product, quotient and chain rules, and speed follows. Take the free JEE Differentiation online test below. It has 15 exam-pattern MCQs with instant scoring. Aim for 12 out of 15.

What JEE asks from differentiation

  • Derivatives from first principles for simple functions.
  • Product, quotient and chain rules in combination.
  • Implicit and logarithmic differentiation.
  • Derivatives of inverse trigonometric forms.
  • Continuity and differentiability of piecewise functions.

Rules to revise first

  • The power rule gives d/dx of x^n as n·x^(n−1).
  • The product rule reads (uv) prime = u prime v + uv prime.
  • The chain rule multiplies the outer and inner derivatives.
  • For y = x^x, take logs first, then differentiate.
  • An even function has an odd derivative, and the reverse holds.

Mistakes that cost JEE marks

  • Dropping u prime v in a hurried product rule.
  • Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule.
  • Assuming a continuous function is always differentiable.

Free JEE Differentiation online test

The 15-question quiz below comes from our verified DPP question bank. It matches the paid e-book question for question. Answer all 15, then press Check my score. Practise the chain rule first, because it hides in most problems.

How to use this test

Set a clock for 30 minutes. Do the plain power-rule ones first. Those are quick marks. Then take on the product and chain rules. Write each step by hand. Do not skip a line. Name the rule before you use it. Check the inner part with care. If an answer looks off, redo it once. Mark every slip you make. Try the set again in two days. Your speed will climb, and your errors will drop. Stay calm. Trust each step. Hard work pays off.

Practise the whole chapter

quiz.title: JEE Differentiation Quiz
quiz.intro: Fifteen exam-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Geometrically, the derivative of y = f(x) at P(a, f(a)) represents:
options: The slope of the tangent to the curve at P
The area under the curve at P
The slope of the normal to the curve at P
questions.explanation: The derivative f prime(a) equals the slope of the tangent line to the curve at x = a.

questions.q: If f is an even differentiable function, then f prime(x) must be:
questions.explanation: Differentiating f(−x) = f(x) gives f prime(−x) = −f prime(x), which defines an odd function.

questions.q: If s(t) is displacement at time t, then s prime(t) represents:
questions.explanation: The rate of change of displacement with time is the instantaneous velocity, ds/dt.

questions.q: A function has a sharp corner at x = c. Which statement holds at x = c?
options: It is both continuous and differentiable
It is differentiable but not continuous
It is neither continuous nor differentiable
It is continuous but not differentiable
questions.explanation: A sharp corner keeps the graph continuous but denies a unique tangent, so the function is not differentiable there.
By the power and sum rules, the derivative is 6x + 5, since the constant term vanishes.
The natural exponential is its own derivative, so d/dx(e^x) = e^x.
Write √x as x^(1/2). The power rule gives (1/2)x^(−1/2) = 1/(2√x).

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = x logₑ x is:
questions.explanation: By the product rule, the derivative is 1·logₑ x + x·(1/x) = logₑ x + 1.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = (sin x)/x is:
questions.explanation: By the quotient rule, the derivative is [x cos x − sin x]/x².

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = e^x/x is:
questions.explanation: By the quotient rule, the derivative is [x e^x − e^x]/x² = e^x(x − 1)/x².

questions.q: The derivative of y = x^x is:
questions.explanation: Take logs to get log y = x log x. Differentiating gives dy/dx = x^x(1 + log x).

questions.q: For s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t, the velocity is zero at:
questions.explanation: Velocity is 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3). It vanishes at t = 1 and t = 3.

questions.q: If f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) for all x, y, with f(0) = 1 and f prime(0) = 2, then f prime(x) equals:
questions.explanation: From first principles, f prime(x) = f(x)·f prime(0) = 2 f(x).

questions.q: If f(x) = ax² + bx for x ≤ 1 and cx + d for x > 1 is differentiable at x = 1, then:
options: Both a + b = c + d and 2a + b = c
questions.explanation: Continuity forces a + b = c + d, and matching derivatives forces 2a + b = c. So both hold.
